newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-ELS IN HISTORIC THIRD SUCCESSIVE MATCHPLAY TITLE SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS IN HISTORIC THIRD SUCCESSIVE MATCHPLAY TITLE SUCCESS.

text.p: Ernie Els carved himself a slice of golfing history on Sunday when he became the first player to capture the World Matchplay title for a third successive year.

The 27-year-old South African top seed beat unseeded Fijian Vijay Singh 3 and 2, defying persistent afternoon rain to remain unbeaten at this event with nine match victories over the past three years.
The world number four's triumph earned him 170,000 pounds ($269,900) and brought his winnings from his three visits to the tournament to a massive 500,000 pounds ($793,900).
Singh, playing in his first final, won 90,000 pounds ($142,900).

In the 33rd edition of the event, Els succeeded at winning his third successive title where his illustrious compatriot Gary Player in 1967, American Hale Irwin in 1976 and Seve Ballesteros twice, in 1983 and 1986, had failed to achieve it.
It all looked some way off on Friday when he trailed American Steve Stricker by six holes before fighting back to win by one.
In Sunday's final Els led by two holes after 17 but lost the last morning hole and the first in the afternoon as Singh drew level.
But Els won the 22nd after Singh drove into trees and three birdies in four holes from the 24th put him in control.
"After the second hole this afternoon I did not play badly. It's a great feeling to win three times in a row. I'm really going to enjoy this," Els said.
U.S. PGA champion Mark Brooks beat British Open titleholder Tom Lehman by one hole in the third place playoff.

Els and Singh, who had just won the 29th to get back to three down, agreed the 483-yard 30th hole had been decisive when the South African hit his second shot into trees while Singh was short of the green in two.
But Els hit his third shot with an eight iron to 30 feet and got down in two putts for a par. Singh, badly needing to win the hole, chipped 12 feet short of the pin and missed the putt.
"That is where I gave the tournament away," Singh, 33, said. "If I had won that hole -- all I needed was a good chip.
"That was the part of my game that let me down. I chipped and putted really poorly today."
"The green was wet and I thought if I hit the ball low it would skip, but it didn't," he explained. "But that is no excuse. It was a poor shot."
Els, who made a birdie four at that hole in the morning after driving into trees, said: "That hole helped me both times, Vijay had a chance for an eagle and a birdie there.
"If he had made birdie in the afternoon it could have been a different story."
They halved the next four holes although Singh missed a chance to prolong the match when he missed from eight feet at the 34th.
Els then closed it out from two feet.

"I played steadily, no heroics. But when I was six down to Steve Stricker after 18 holes on Friday, winning the tournament never crossed my mind. I was playing with no confidence and I was just hanging on.
"Then I chipped in a couple of times and made a few putts and managed to win it. Then yesterday against Mark Brooks, it was a total cruise," he said. He beat Brooks 10 and 8.

"I did not play as well this year as I did the last two years," Els said. I think last year I was 25 under par and this time only 12 or 13. But the weather has not been as good this year, with wind and rain today."
Els finally went in front to stay at the 22nd hole where Singh drove into trees and conceded.
Then Els won the 24th with a nine-foot birdie, the next with a par after Singh again drove into trees and the 26th with a 10- footer for birdie to go four ahead.
After Els struck his second at the 27th to one foot, Singh saved himself by hitting his to five feet and holing for a half.
Then he won the 29th with a sand wedge approach to two feet.
But his failure at the next was his last chance to strike a blow at the South African.
Both players had six birdies on the day but Singh made four bogeys, one more than he made altogether in his first three matches.
Singh lost all four of the holes he bogeyed. "I made too many mistakes and gave away too many holes," he said. "I would like to play it over again if I could."
